claims.source: Recent work in computational cognitive science has shown DPPs naturally capture inductive biases in human inference, such as some word-learning and reasoning tasks (e.g., one noun should only refer to one object) while also serving as an eﬃcient memory code (Webb et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Orthogonal coding has been proposed to be characteristic of representations in mammalian hippocampus and integral for episodic memory.
claims.source: DPPs also provide a formal objective for the type of orthogonal coding that has been proposed to be characteristic of representations in mammalian hippocampus, and integral for episodic memory (McClelland et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to neuroscience literature.

claims.claim: Grid cell code is implemented in the entorhinal cortex, one synapse upstream of the hippocampus.
claims.source: Thus, using the DPP objective to govern attention over the grid cell code, known to be implemented in the entorhinal cortex (Hafting et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2007; Stensola et al., 2012; Giocomo et al., 2011; Brandon et al., 2011) (one synapse upstream of the hippocampus), aligns with the function and organization of cognitive and neural systems underlying the capability for abstraction.
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claims.claim: The network was trained on 80% of all sets of points in the training range, with 20% held out as the validation set.
claims.source: The network was trained on 80% of all such sets of points in the training range, with 20% held out as the validation set.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: The total number of discrete frequencies in the entorhinal cortex has been estimated to be between 8 and 12.
claims.source: Empirically, it has been estimated to be between 8 and 12 (Moser et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to empirical neuroscience work.

claims.claim: Higher-frequency grid cell embeddings exhibit greater variance over the training data than lower-frequency embeddings.
claims.source: We ﬁnd that grid cell embeddings corresponding to the higher spatial frequency grid cells exhibit greater variance over the training data than the lower-frequency embeddings, while at the same time the correlations among those grid cell embeddings are lower than the correlations among the lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claims.claim: Correlations among higher-frequency grid cell embeddings are lower than correlations among lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
claims.source: We ﬁnd that grid cell embeddings corresponding to the higher spatial frequency grid cells exhibit greater variance over the training data than the lower-frequency embeddings, while at the same time the correlations among those grid cell embeddings are lower than the correlations among the lower-frequency grid cell embeddings.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claims.claim: The determinant of the covariance matrix of grid cell embeddings is maximized when the variances are high and the correlation among embeddings is low.
claims.source: The determinant of the covariance matrix of the grid cell embeddings is maximized when the variances of the grid cell embeddings are high (they are 'expressive') and the correlation among the grid cell embeddings is low (they 'cover the representational space').
claims.evidence: This is based on mathematical properties of determinants and covariance matrices.

claims.claim: Higher-frequency grid cell embeddings more efficiently cover the representational space of the training data.
claims.source: As a result, the higher-frequency grid cell embeddings more eﬃciently cover the representational space of the training data, allowing them to eﬃciently capture the same relational structure across training and test distributions which is required for OOD generalization.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical properties and empirical observations.

claims.claim: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect accuracy on all test regions for the analogy task using an LSTM inference module.
claims.source: DPP-A (shown in blue) achieves nearly perfect accuracy on all of the test regions, considerably outperforming the other models.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: Using all grid cell code with no DPP-A led to the worst OOD generalization performance for translation in the analogy task.
claims.source: For the case of translation, using all the grid cell code with no DPP-A (shown in purple) led to the worst OOD generalization performance, overﬁtting on the training set.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 experimental results.

claims.claim: DPP-A substantially outperformed all other models for scaling in the analogy task, with a nearly 70% improvement in average test accuracy.
claims.source: For the case of scaling, locked dropout and L1 regularization performed slightly better than TCN, achieving marginally higher test accuracy, but DPP-A still substantially outperformed all other models, with a nearly 70% improvement in average test accuracy.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: With no DPP-A, the transformer did poorly on analogies on the test regions.
claims.source: With no explicit attention (no DPP-A) over the grid cell code (shown in orange), the transformer did poorly on the analogies on the test regions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 experimental results.

claims.claim: Simply using a more sophisticated architecture with standard forms of attention is not sufficient to enable OOD generalization based on grid cell code.
claims.source: This suggests that simply using a more sophisticated architecture with standard forms of attention is not suﬃcient to enable OOD generalization based on the grid cell code.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with transformers.

claims.claim: With DPP-A, the OOD generalization performance of the transformer is nearly perfect for both translation and scaling on the analogy task.
claims.source: With DPP-A (shown in blue), the OOD generalization performance of the transformer is nearly perfect for both translation and scaling.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: Grid cell code coupled with DPP-A can be exploited for OOD generalization effectively by different architectures.
claims.source: These results also demonstrate that grid cell code coupled with DPP-A can be exploited for OOD generalization eﬀectively by diﬀerent architectures.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from results with both LSTM and transformer architectures.

claims.claim: DPP-A achieves higher accuracy for addition than multiplication on the test regions in the arithmetic task.
claims.source: DPP-A achieves higher accuracy for addition than multiplication on the test regions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 experimental results.

claims.claim: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition in the arithmetic task.
claims.source: However, in both cases DPP-A signiﬁcantly outperforms the other models, achieving nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition, and 65% accuracy for multiplication, compared with under 20% accuracy for all the other models.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: DPP-A achieves 65% accuracy for multiplication in the arithmetic task, compared with under 20% accuracy for all other models.
claims.source: However, in both cases DPP-A signiﬁcantly outperforms the other models, achieving nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition, and 65% accuracy for multiplication, compared with under 20% accuracy for all the other models.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: Grid cell embeddings obtained after the first step in Algorithm 1 are not able to fully preserve the relational structure for multiplication problems on the test regions.
claims.source: We found that grid cell embeddings obtained after the ﬁrst step in Algorithm 1 are not able to fully preserve the relational structure for multiplication problems on the test regions (more details in Appendix 1: 'Why is OOD generalization performance worse for the multiplication task?'), but still it aﬀords superior capacity for OOD generalization than any of the other models.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding from the experiments.

claims.claim: With no DPP-A, the transformer achieved around 20–30% accuracy on addition and multiplication on the test regions.
claims.source: With no DPP-A over the grid cell code the transformer did poorly on addition and multiplication on the test regions, achieving around 20–30% accuracy.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 experimental results.

claims.claim: With DPP-A, the transformer's OOD generalization performance is nearly perfect for addition in the arithmetic task.
claims.source: With DPP-A, the OOD generalization performance of the transformer shows a pattern similar to that for LSTM: it is nearly perfect for addition
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: With DPP-A, the transformer shows approximately 40% better performance than without DPP-A on multiplication.
claims.source: and, though not as good on multiplication, nevertheless shows approximately 40% better performance than the transformer multiplication.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing experimental results.

claims.claim: The average accuracy on test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder.
claims.source: The average accuracy on the test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder (shown in green) is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder (shown in orange), but both still achieve signiﬁcantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code which support perfect OOD generalization.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing ablation study results.

claims.claim: Both one-hot and smoothed one-hot embeddings achieve significantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code.
claims.source: The average accuracy on the test regions for translation and scaling using smoothed one-hots passed through an encoder (shown in green) is nearly 30% better than simple one-hot embeddings passed through an encoder (shown in orange), but both still achieve signiﬁcantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code which support perfect OOD generalization.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing ablation study results.

claims.claim: For translation, the average accuracy over test regions using grid cell code is nearly 25% more compared to other embeddings.
claims.source: For translation (left), the average accuracy over the test regions using grid cell code (shown in blue) is nearly 25% more compared to other embeddings, which all yield performance near chance (∼15%).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8 showing ablation study results.

claims.claim: Grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insufficient to promote OOD generalization.
claims.source: However, despite their intrinsic structure, we ﬁnd that grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insuﬃcient to promote OOD generalization, and standard approaches for preventing overﬁtting oﬀer only modest gains.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental results comparing different methods.

claims.claim: Standard approaches for preventing overfitting offer only modest gains in OOD generalization.
claims.source: However, despite their intrinsic structure, we ﬁnd that grid cell code and standard error-driven learning alone are insuﬃcient to promote OOD generalization, and standard approaches for preventing overﬁtting oﬀer only modest gains.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental comparisons with dropout and L1 regularization.

claims.claim: The combination of grid cell code and DPP-A promotes OOD generalization across both translation and scale when incorporated into LSTM and transformer architectures.
claims.source: This is addressed by the second component, using DPP-A to implement attentional regularization over the grid cell code. DPP-A allows only a relevant and diverse subset of cells to inﬂuence downstream computation in the inference module using the statistics of the training data. For proof of concept, we started with two challenging cognitive tasks (analogy and arithmetic), and showed that the combination of grid cell code and DPP-A promotes OOD generalization across both translation and scale when incorporated into common architectures (LSTM and transformer).
claims.evidence: This is the main finding demonstrated through experiments.

claims.claim: The DPP-A attentional mechanism is different from the attentional mechanism in the transformer module.
claims.source: It is worth noting that the DPP-A attentional mechanism is diﬀerent from the attentional mechanism in the transformer module, and both are needed for strong OOD generalization in the case of transformers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing both mechanisms are necessary.

claims.claim: Use of standard self-attention in transformers over inputs in place of DPP-A would lead to weightings of grid cell embeddings over all frequencies and phases.
claims.source: Use of the standard self-attention mechanism in transformers over the inputs (i.e., A, B, C, and D for the analogy task) in place of DPP-A would lead to weightings of grid cell embeddings over all frequencies and phases.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from understanding of how transformer attention works.

claims.claim: The objective function for DPP-A selectively assigns the greatest weight to all grid cell embeddings of the frequency for which the determinant of the covariance matrix is greatest.
claims.source: The objective function for the DPP-A represents an inductive bias, that selectively assigns the greatest weight to all grid cell embeddings (i.e., for all phases) of the frequency for which the determinant of the covariance matrix is greatest computed over the training space.
claims.evidence: This describes how the DPP-A mechanism works based on its mathematical formulation.

claims.claim: Grid cell code can be derived using standard analytical techniques for dimensionality reduction.
claims.source: A body of recent computational work has shown that representations similar to grid cells can be derived using standard analytical techniques for dimensionality reduction (Dordek et al., 2016; Stachenfeld et al., 2017), as well as from error-driven learning paradigms (Cueva and Wei, 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Whittington et al., 2020; Sorscher et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior computational work.

claims.claim: Grid cells emerge in networks trained to generalize to novel location/object combinations and support transitive inference.
claims.source: Previous work has also shown that grid cells emerge in networks trained to generalize to novel location/object combinations, and support transitive inference (Whittington et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: DPPs have been used for supervised video summarization.
claims.source: In the ﬁeld of machine learning, DPPs have been used for supervised video summarization (Gong et al., 2014), diverse recommendations (Chen et al., 2018), selecting a subset of diverse neurons to prune a neural network without hurting performance (Mariet and Sra, 2015), and diverse minibatch attention for stochastic gradient descent (Zhang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claims.claim: DPPs have not previously been combined with grid cell code for OOD generalization.
claims.source: To our knowledge, however, DPPs have not previously been combined with the grid cell code that we employ here, and have not been used to enable OOD generalization.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work.

claims.claim: Weight decay is a commonly employed technique to prevent deep learning systems from overfitting.
claims.source: Various approaches have been proposed to prevent deep learning systems from overﬁtting, and enable them to generalize. A commonly employed technique is weight decay (Krogh and Hertz, 1992).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claims.claim: Dropout is a regularization technique which reduces overfitting by randomly zeroing units from the neural network during training.
claims.source: Srivastava et al., 2014 proposed dropout, a regularization technique which reduces overﬁtting by randomly zeroing units from the neural network during training.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claims.claim: The prefrontal cortex encodes and actively maintains abstract information needed for task performance such as rules and relations.
claims.source: In particular, the role of the prefrontal cortex in the encoding and active maintenance of abstract information needed for task performance (such as rules and relations) has often been modeled using gated recurrent networks, such as LSTMs (Frank et al., 2001; Braver and Cohen, 2000)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claims.claim: The posterior parietal cortex supports 'maps' that may provide an important substrate for computing complex relations.
claims.source: and the posterior parietal cortex has long been known to support 'maps' that may provide an important substrate for computing complex relations (Summerfield et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to neuroscience literature.

claims.claim: The model predicts that high-frequency grid cells should increase their firing rate more than low-frequency cells when individuals are exposed to a task requiring consistent exposure to a subregion.
claims.source: This could be tested experimentally by exposing individuals (e.g., rodents or humans) to a task that requires consistent exposure to a subregion, and evaluating the distribution of activity over the grid cells. Our model predicts that high-frequency grid cells should increase their ﬁring rate more than low-frequency cells, since the high-frequency grid cells maximize the determinant of the covariance matrix of the grid cell embeddings.
claims.evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the model.

claims.claim: Bozkurt et al., 2022 proposed a biologically plausible neural network algorithm using a weighted similarity matrix approach to implement a determinant maximization criterion.
claims.source: In that regard, Bozkurt et al., 2022 recently proposed a biologically plausible neural network algorithm using a weighted similarity matrix approach to implement a determinant maximization criterion, which is the core idea underlying the objective function we use for DPP-A (Equation 6), suggesting that the DPP-A mechanism we describe may also be biologically plausible.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to recent work on biological plausibility.

claims.claim: Frankland and Cohen, 2020 suggested that the use of DPPs may help explain a mutual exclusivity bias observed in human word learning and reasoning.
claims.source: It is also worth noting that Frankland and Cohen, 2020 have suggested that the use of DPPs may also help explain a mutual exclusivity bias observed in human word learning and reasoning.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM) model suggests that grid cells in the medial entorhinal may form a basis set that captures structural knowledge for nonlinear spaces.
claims.source: The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM) model (Whittington et al., 2020) suggests that grid cells in the medial entorhinal may form a basis set that captures structural knowledge for such nonlinear spaces, such as social hierarchies and transitive inference when formalized as a connected graph.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Eigen decomposition of the successor representation provides an abstract structured representation of a space that is analogous to grid cell code.
claims.source: Another would be to use eigen decomposition of the successor representation (Dayan, 1993), a learnable predictive representation of possible future states that has been shown by Stachenfeld et al., 2017 to provide an abstract structured representation of a space that is analogous to the grid cell code.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

results.result: Deep neural networks have achieved human-level or superior performance in many domains but fail to generalize beyond their training conditions, falling short of human-like strong generalization capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C10 establish the success of DNNs in specific domains with proper citations, while C3 and C11 document their limitations in generalization, also supported by citations to prior work. These claims collectively establish the motivation for the study.

results.result: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is defined as successful performance on test examples outside the training distribution.
results.evaluation: C4 provides a standard definitional claim based on established machine learning terminology, which is well-accepted in the field.

results.result: Grid cells in the mammalian entorhinal cortex encode metric spaces using periodic representations with properties of translation and scale invariance across frequencies, with 8-12 discrete frequencies empirically observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C14, C15, C21, and C31 describe well-established neuroscience findings about grid cells, all supported by multiple citations to empirical neuroscience literature. These properties are foundational to the proposed method.

results.result: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) originated in physics, have been adopted in machine learning for diversity-based selection, capture human cognitive biases, and formalize orthogonal coding in hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 describe the background and applications of DPPs, all supported by appropriate citations to physics, machine learning, and neuroscience literature. This establishes the theoretical foundation for DPP-A.

results.result: DPP-A is an attention mechanism that maximizes coverage of representational space by attending to high-variance, low-correlation grid cell embeddings, with higher-frequency embeddings showing these properties and more efficiently covering the training data representational space.
results.evaluation: C7 defines DPP-A, while C34-C37 provide empirical observations and mathematical justification. C36 is mathematically sound (determinant properties), and C34-C35 report experimental findings. C37 logically follows from the mathematical properties and observations.

results.result: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect OOD generalization accuracy on analogy tasks with LSTM inference modules for both translation and scaling, substantially outperforming baseline methods including no attention (which overfits), dropout, L1 regularization, and TCN.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 report experimental results shown in Figure 3 with quantitative comparisons. The results show clear performance differences with DPP-A achieving ~100% accuracy versus 20-70% for other methods. Three networks were trained per condition with error bars reported.

results.result: Transformers without DPP-A perform poorly on OOD analogy tasks, but with DPP-A achieve nearly perfect generalization for both translation and scaling, demonstrating that grid cell code with DPP-A enables OOD generalization across different architectures.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 report transformer results from Figure 4. C45 and C47 present empirical findings, C46 is a reasonable inference from the data, and C48 generalizes across both LSTM and transformer results. The comparison is methodologically sound.

results.result: DPP-A achieves nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition (~100% accuracy) and moderate performance for multiplication (65% accuracy) with LSTM, substantially outperforming other methods (<20% accuracy), though grid cell embeddings cannot fully preserve relational structure for multiplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 report arithmetic task results from Figure 5. The quantitative results are clearly presented with appropriate comparisons. C52 acknowledges a limitation with reference to additional analysis in the appendix, which is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: Transformers with DPP-A achieve nearly perfect OOD generalization for addition and ~40% improvement over baseline for multiplication on arithmetic tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 report transformer arithmetic results from Figure 6, showing consistent patterns with LSTM results. The quantitative improvements are clearly documented with appropriate experimental controls.

results.result: Ablation studies show that smoothed one-hot embeddings with DPP-A perform ~30% better than simple one-hot embeddings but both achieve significantly lower test accuracy than grid cell code, with grid cell code showing ~25% higher accuracy for translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 report ablation study results from Figures 7-8 comparing different embedding schemes. The quantitative comparisons are clear, though limited to only 2-3 test regions due to computational constraints, which is acknowledged.

results.result: Grid cell code alone is insufficient for OOD generalization, standard regularization methods offer only modest gains, but combining grid cell code with DPP-A promotes strong OOD generalization across translation and scale in both LSTM and transformer architectures.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 synthesize the main findings. C59 and C60 are supported by comparisons in Figures 3-6 showing poor performance without DPP-A or with standard regularization. C61 represents the central finding supported by all experimental results.

results.result: DPP-A attention differs from transformer self-attention and both are necessary for strong OOD generalization; DPP-A selectively weights grid cell embeddings of the frequency with maximum covariance matrix determinant, while standard self-attention would weight all frequencies and phases.
results.evaluation: C62 is supported by experimental results showing both mechanisms are needed (Figures 4, 6). C63 and C64 provide mechanistic explanations based on the mathematical formulation and are logically sound inferences from the algorithm design.

results.result: Temporal context normalization (TCN) enables OOD generalization by preserving relational structure within local temporal contexts while abstracting over differences between contexts.
results.evaluation: C16 accurately describes prior work (Webb et al., 2020) with appropriate citation. This establishes a baseline comparison method for the current study.

results.result: Grid cell representations can emerge from dimensionality reduction techniques and error-driven learning, and support generalization to novel combinations and transitive inference.
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C66 accurately summarize prior computational work with appropriate citations, establishing that grid cell code can be learned rather than hand-crafted.

results.result: DPPs have been used in machine learning for various applications including video summarization and neural network pruning, but have not previously been combined with grid cell code for OOD generalization.
results.evaluation: C67 accurately cites prior DPP applications in machine learning. C68 claims novelty, which appears reasonable given the literature review, though comprehensive verification of novelty claims is inherently difficult.

results.result: Weight decay and dropout are commonly employed regularization techniques to prevent overfitting in deep learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 accurately describe standard machine learning techniques with appropriate citations, establishing baseline comparison methods.

results.result: The prefrontal cortex encodes abstract task information and has been modeled with LSTMs, while posterior parietal cortex supports maps for computing complex relations.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C72 accurately summarize neuroscience findings with appropriate citations, providing biological motivation for the inference module architecture choices.

results.result: The model predicts that high-frequency grid cells should increase firing rates more than low-frequency cells during tasks requiring consistent exposure to a subregion.
results.evaluation: C73 presents a testable prediction derived from the model's mechanism. While the prediction logically follows from the DPP-A objective, it remains untested and speculative. The prediction is reasonable but requires experimental validation.

results.result: Recent work suggests biologically plausible implementations of determinant maximization and that DPPs may explain cognitive biases in human reasoning.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 accurately cite recent work suggesting biological plausibility and cognitive relevance of DPPs, strengthening the theoretical motivation for the approach.

results.result: Alternative approaches including the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine and successor representation eigen decomposition can provide structured representations analogous to grid cell code for nonlinear spaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 accurately describe alternative approaches from prior work with appropriate citations, acknowledging potential extensions of the current framework.

results.result: A loss function combining task-optimized error with DPP-A can exploit recurring motifs in grid cell code and integrate with common architectures to achieve strong OOD generalization on analogy and arithmetic tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 summarize the main methodological contribution and are supported by the comprehensive experimental results across multiple tasks and architectures (Figures 3-6). The two-step training algorithm is clearly described.

results.result: Networks were trained on 80% of training data with 20% held out for validation.
results.evaluation: C23 describes standard experimental methodology for train/validation splits, which is appropriate and clearly documented.

results.result: The combination of grid cell code with DPP-A enables strong out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on analogy tasks across both translation and scaling transformations. DPP-A achieves nearly perfect accuracy on all test regions, substantially outperforming baseline models (nearly 70% improvement for scaling), and this performance generalizes across both LSTM and transformer architectures.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The first reviewer states the work 'provides compelling evidence that the model can improve generalization performance for analogies' and calls it 'important modeling work.' The second reviewer confirms 'the authors present simulations results demonstrating this model can perform out-of-distribution generalisation' and has 'no issues with the technical details.'

results.result: DPP-A achieves strong OOD generalization on arithmetic tasks, with nearly perfect performance for addition and 65% accuracy for multiplication using LSTM (compared to under 20% for other models). With transformers, DPP-A shows nearly perfect performance for addition and approximately 40% better performance than without DPP-A on multiplication.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly states the simulations 'provide compelling evidence that the model can improve generalization performance for...addition, and multiplication.' The second reviewer confirms the model demonstrates OOD generalization and raises no concerns about the arithmetic task results.

results.result: Grid cell code alone without DPP-A is insufficient for OOD generalization, and standard regularization approaches (dropout, L1 regularization, TCN) offer only modest improvements. Simply using sophisticated architectures with standard attention mechanisms does not enable OOD generalization based on grid cell code.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these comparative findings without challenge. The first reviewer acknowledges the work demonstrates how grid cell codes 'combined with an attentional mechanism' achieve generalization, implicitly accepting that the combination is necessary. The second reviewer explicitly notes the model works 'when combined with a domain adaptation mechanism, like DPP-A.'

results.result: Higher-frequency grid cell embeddings exhibit greater variance and lower correlations than lower-frequency embeddings, maximizing the determinant of the covariance matrix. This allows higher-frequency grid cells to more efficiently cover the representational space and capture relational structure across training and test distributions.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not question this mechanistic explanation of how DPP-A works. The second reviewer explicitly states they have 'no issues with the technical details' and acknowledges the paper 'nicely demonstrates how neural codes can be transformed into a common representational space,' implicitly accepting the mathematical properties described.

results.result: Ablation studies show that grid cell code substantially outperforms alternative embeddings (one-hot and smoothed one-hot encodings) for OOD generalization. Grid cell code achieves nearly 25-30% higher accuracy on test regions compared to these alternatives.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these ablation results without critique. The first reviewer's statement that the work provides 'compelling evidence' for the model's performance implicitly includes acceptance of the ablation studies that support the necessity of grid cell code. The second reviewer raises no concerns about the technical comparisons.

results.result: Grid cell embeddings are not able to fully preserve relational structure for multiplication problems on test regions, though they still afford superior OOD generalization capacity compared to other models.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not challenge this limitation. The first reviewer acknowledges the model improves performance on multiplication without questioning the incomplete preservation of relational structure. The second reviewer confirms the model performs OOD generalization without raising concerns about this specific limitation.

results.result: The DPP-A attentional mechanism is functionally distinct from standard transformer self-attention, and both mechanisms are necessary for strong OOD generalization in transformers. DPP-A selectively assigns weight to grid cell embeddings based on maximizing the determinant of the covariance matrix, rather than weighting across all frequencies and phases.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept this mechanistic distinction without challenge. The second reviewer explicitly notes the authors 'use DPP-A which is, in this context, a mechanism of adapting to input scale changes,' acknowledging the specific functional role of DPP-A distinct from standard attention.

results.result: Grid cells in the mammalian entorhinal cortex represent metric spaces through abstract representations of relational structure organized in recurring motifs. These representations exhibit translation invariance within frequencies and scale invariance across frequencies due to their periodic response properties.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these neuroscience background claims without question. The first reviewer describes the work as demonstrating 'how neural grid codes can support human-like generalization capabilities,' accepting the biological basis. The second reviewer explicitly acknowledges 'the representational basis is grid-cell codes' and discusses their multi-scale and translational invariance properties.

results.result: Deep neural networks have achieved human-level performance in many domains but fall short of strong forms of generalization characteristic of human intelligence, particularly for out-of-distribution scenarios. Their success is generally limited to the narrow conditions under which they were trained.
results.evaluation: The reviewers implicitly accept this motivating context. The first reviewer describes the work as 'significant in demonstrating how neural grid codes can support human-like generalization capabilities,' acknowledging the gap the work addresses. The second reviewer frames the work as addressing 'out-of-distribution generalisation,' accepting the premise that this is a challenge for current models.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on motivation claims (C1, C2, C3, C10, C11). Both evaluations find these claims about DNN successes and limitations well-supported, establishing the study's rationale.
Perfect agreement on ablation study results (C56, C57, C58). Both evaluations accept the comparative findings showing grid cell code superiority over alternative embedding schemes.
Perfect agreement on mechanistic claims (C62, C63, C64). Both evaluations support the explanation of how DPP-A provides domain adaptation distinct from standard attention mechanisms.

Strong agreement on neuroscience background (C5, C6, C14, C15, C21). Both evaluations accept grid cell properties as well-established. OpenEval also includes C31 which peer review doesn't explicitly address.

Strong agreement on DPP-A mechanism (C34, C35, C36, C37). Both evaluations accept the mathematical properties and empirical observations. OpenEval also includes C7 (DPP-A definition) which peer review doesn't separately evaluate.

Both address main methodological contribution (C8, C9). OpenEval focuses on the two-step training algorithm description, while peer review emphasizes the overall performance improvements (also covering C42, C44, C47, C48, C61).
Partial overlap on analogy task results. OpenEval R6 covers C42, C43, C44 from Figure 3, while peer R1 includes C42, C44 along with broader claims about overall model performance.
Partial overlap on transformer results. OpenEval R7 addresses C45-C48 from Figure 4, while peer R1 includes C47, C48 as part of broader validation of the model's generalization capabilities.
Partial overlap on transformer findings. OpenEval R7 covers C45, C46 (transformer-specific results), while peer R3 includes these claims within broader comparative analysis (C43, C45, C46, C59, C60).
Partial overlap on arithmetic tasks. OpenEval R8 addresses LSTM arithmetic results (C49-C52), while peer R2 focuses on both LSTM and transformer arithmetic (C50, C51, C54, C55).
Partial overlap on transformer arithmetic. OpenEval R9 covers C53-C55 from Figure 6, while peer R2 includes C54, C55 along with LSTM results (C50, C51).
